from: It is unlawful to sell, license or otherwise provide a coordinated pricing algorithm to Berkeley landlords, and unlawful for a landlord to use one, to set or recommend rents or occupancy levels for residential units in Berkeley. Each unit and each month of a violation is a separate violation, and both the City Attorney and aggrieved tenants may sue for injunctive relief, damages and civil penalties.
to: It is unlawful to sell, license or otherwise provide a coordinated pricing algorithm to Berkeley landlords, and unlawful for a landlord to use one, to set or recommend rents or occupancy levels for residential units in Berkeley; each unit and each month of use is a separate violation. The City Attorney may sue over either the sale or the use, and an aggrieved tenant may sue a landlord over its use, for injunctive relief, damages and civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation.

from: Rental housing providers may not ask about or use criminal history or criminal background checks in rental advertising, applications, tenant selection, or decision-making. Prohibited acts include: inquiring about criminal history; indicating that persons with criminal backgrounds will not be considered; refusing to rent or terminating a tenancy based on criminal history; requiring disclosure or authorization for release of criminal history; demanding a higher security deposit or rent based on criminal history; refusing to allow an immediate family member to be added based on that person's criminal history; disqualifying tenants from rental assistance programs such as Section 8 based on criminal history; and treating applicants or tenants differently based on criminal history. If a landlord takes any action against an applicant or tenant based on criminal history, the landlord must provide written notice and an opportunity to respond. Housing providers must post a prescribed Notice to Rental Applicants and Tenants prominently on application materials, websites, and frequently visited locations under their control.
to: Berkeley rental housing providers may not ask about or use criminal history or background checks in advertising, applications, tenant selection or tenancy decisions; this includes refusing to rent, terminating a tenancy, charging a higher deposit or rent, refusing to add an immediate family member, or treating applicants or tenants differently because of criminal history. Any action taken against an applicant or tenant based on criminal history requires written notice and an opportunity to respond.

from: Landlords of units subject to the Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance must pay tenants interest on security deposits. Interest accrues monthly at a rate set annually by the City. The landlord must pay accrued interest either monthly or yearly, as a direct payment or as a credit against rent. The landlord chooses the method and must notify the tenant in writing. Waiting until the end of the tenancy to pay the interest with the deposit refund does not satisfy the ordinance.
to: Landlords of units under the Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance must pay tenants security deposit interest, which accrues monthly at a rate the City sets each year. The interest must be paid monthly or yearly, either directly or as a rent credit, in a method the landlord chooses and states to the tenant in writing; paying it only with the deposit refund at move-out does not comply.

from: Tenancies in RSO units may be ended only for legal at-fault or no-fault reasons. For a no-fault eviction the landlord must first file a Declaration of Intent to Evict with LAHD, give the required written notice, and pay relocation assistance within 15 days of serving notice (or place it in escrow). Termination notices must be filed with LAHD within 3 business days of service.
to: Tenancies in RSO units may be ended only for legal at-fault or no-fault reasons. For a no-fault eviction the landlord must first file a Declaration of Intent to Evict with LAHD, give the required written notice, and pay relocation assistance within 15 days of serving notice (or place it in escrow). A copy of the termination notice must be filed with LAHD no later than 3 days after it is served.

from: A security deposit may not exceed the first month's rent. It must be held in a separate interest-bearing Massachusetts bank account, and the tenant must get a receipt within 30 days naming the bank, location, amount and account number. The tenant must get a signed receipt when the deposit is received, and a written statement of the premises' condition within 10 days after tenancy commences or on receipt of the deposit, whichever is later. If the lessor holds the deposit for a year or longer, it must pay interest at 5% per year (or the lesser amount actually received from the bank) at the end of each year of the tenancy. The lessor must return the deposit, less permitted deductions, within 30 days after the tenancy ends. Permitted deductions are unpaid rent or water charges, unpaid tax increases under a conforming escalation clause, and reasonable repair of damage beyond normal wear and tear. Damage deductions require a sworn itemized list with cost evidence within the same 30 days. The lessor must keep deposit records for 2 years after the tenancy ends. The deposit and accrued interest must be transferred to a successor in interest. As amended effective Aug 1, 2025, the Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities may by regulation authorize an optional fee in lieu of a security deposit, capped at 1 month's rent in total with any deposit.
to: A landlord may not take a security deposit larger than the first month's rent and must hold it in a separate interest-bearing Massachusetts bank account, give the tenant a receipt naming the bank, amount and account number within 30 days, and, if it holds the deposit for 1 year or longer, pay interest at 5% per year (or the lesser rate the bank paid) each year of the tenancy. Within 30 days after the tenancy ends, the landlord must return the deposit, deducting only unpaid rent or water charges, unpaid tax-escalation amounts, or reasonable repair costs for damage beyond normal wear and tear, which must be supported by a sworn itemized list with cost evidence; since Aug 1, 2025, state regulations may allow an optional fee in lieu of a deposit, capped at 1 month's rent.

from: It is an unlawful practice for any person furnishing credit, services or rental accommodations to discriminate against an individual who receives federal, state or local public assistance (including medical assistance), or who is a tenant receiving federal, state or local housing subsidies (including rental assistance or rental supplements). The ban applies whether the discrimination is because the individual is such a recipient or because of any requirement of the assistance or subsidy program. Subsection 7B separately bars rental notices, statements or advertisements that indicate a preference, limitation or discrimination based on public assistance recipiency.
to: Anyone furnishing credit, services or rental accommodations may not discriminate against an individual who receives federal, state or local public assistance (including medical assistance) or who is a tenant receiving federal, state or local housing subsidies (including rental assistance or rental supplements). This applies whether the discrimination is because the person is such a recipient or because of any requirement of the assistance or subsidy program.

from: N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 et seq.

Eligible senior, disabled or disabled-veteran tenants in a building being converted to a condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership may be protected from eviction for up to 40 years if they apply, generally within 60 days. The 1992 Tenant Protection Act extends these protections to qualified tenants in Hudson County.
to: In a building being converted to a condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership, eligible senior (62+), permanently disabled, or 60%+ service-disabled veteran tenants who meet the income limit and apply (generally within 60 days) may be protected from eviction for 40 years. The Tenant Protection Act of 1992 gives additional protected tenancy to qualified tenants in Hudson County (currently the only qualified county) who are not eligible as seniors or disabled persons.

from: A landlord or agent may not require an application or similar fee to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes that exceeds $50. Beginning January 1 of the year next following enactment and each year after, the cap is adjusted in proportion to the percent change in the CPI (NY-Northern NJ-Long Island, All Urban Consumers, All Items) over the 12 months ending October 31 of the prior year. The adjustment is made only if the change is greater than zero. The Director of the Division of Consumer Affairs publishes the applicable limit annually on the division's website and adopts implementing rules, including a mechanism for applicants to report violations. The amount wrongfully charged is taken from the collected penalty and remitted to the applicant or prospective tenant.
to: A landlord or agent may not charge an application or similar fee over $50 to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental unit. Beginning January 1, 2027, the cap is adjusted annually for CPI increases only (the Division of Consumer Affairs publishes the limit). Violations carry penalties up to $500/$750/$1,000, and the overcharge is refunded to the applicant.

from: $50 maximum application fee, adjusted annually by CPI

from: Landlords of covered units may raise rent only once every 12 months, by no more than the lesser of 3% or 80% of the percent change in the CPI over the most recent 12-month period, and no increase is permitted if the CPI change is negative. The City publishes the allowable increase by June 30 each year, effective September 1, and owners may petition for a larger increase needed for a fair and reasonable return.
